verses.text: Early in the morning, all the chief priests and the elders of the people made their plans to have Jesus put to death.
They tied him up, led him away and handed him over to Pilate, the governor.
Judas, who had handed Jesus over, saw that Jesus had been sentenced to death. He was filled with regret, and he brought the thirty silver coins back to the chief priests and the elders.
He said, "I have sinned. I have handed over an innocent man to be killed." "What do we care?" they replied. "That is your problem."
So Judas threw the money into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself.
The chief priests picked up the coins. They said, "It is against the law to put this money into the temple treasury, because it is money paid for blood."
So they decided to use the money to buy the potter's field, as a place to bury people who were not from there.
That is why it has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
Then what the prophet Jeremiah had said came true: "They took the thirty silver coins, the price the people of Israel had set on him.
And they used them to buy the potter's field, as the Lord had commanded me."
Meanwhile Jesus stood in front of the governor. The governor asked him, "Are you the king of the Jews?" "You have said so," Jesus replied.
When the chief priests and the elders accused him, he did not answer.
Then Pilate asked him, "Do you not hear all the things they are accusing you of?"
But Jesus did not answer even one question, and the governor was very amazed.
It was the governor's custom at the festival to set free one prisoner chosen by the crowd.
At that time they had a well-known prisoner named Barabbas.
So when the crowd had gathered, Pilate asked them, "Which one do you want me to set free for you? Barabbas, or Jesus who is called the Christ?"
He knew it was because they were jealous that the leaders had handed Jesus over to him.
While Pilate was sitting in the judge's seat, his wife sent him a message. It said, "Do not have anything to do with that innocent man. I have suffered a great deal today in a dream because of him."
But the chief priests and the elders talked the crowd into asking for Barabbas and having Jesus put to death.
"Which of the two do you want me to set free for you?" asked the governor. "Barabbas," they answered.
"Then what should I do with Jesus who is called the Christ?" Pilate asked. They all answered, "Nail him to a cross!"
"Why? What wrong has he done?" asked Pilate. But they shouted even louder, "Nail him to a cross!"

Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, and that a riot was starting. So he took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd. "I am not guilty of this man's death," he said. "It is your responsibility!"
All the people answered, "Let the blame for his death be on us and on our children!"
Then Pilate set Barabbas free for them. He had Jesus whipped, and then he handed him over to be nailed to a cross.
Then the governor's soldiers took Jesus into the governor's palace. The whole company of soldiers gathered around him.
They took off his clothes and put a red robe on him.
Then they twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head. They put a stick in his right hand. Then they knelt in front of him and made fun of him. "Hail, king of the Jews!" they said.
They spat on him. They took the stick and hit him on the head again and again.
After they had made fun of him, they took off the robe and put his own clothes back on him. Then they led him away to nail him to a cross.
As they were going out, they met a man from Cyrene named Simon, and they forced him to carry the cross.
They came to a place called Golgotha, which means the Place of the Skull.
There they offered Jesus wine to drink, mixed with a bitter liquid. But after tasting it, he refused to drink it.
When they had nailed him to the cross, they divided up his clothes by throwing dice.
Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.
Above his head they put up the written charge against him: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Two robbers were nailed to crosses with him, one on his right and one on his left.
People who passed by shouted insults at him, shaking their heads.
They said, "You were going to destroy the temple and build it again in three days. So save yourself! Come down from the cross, if you are the Son of God!"
In the same way the chief priests, the teachers of the law and the elders made fun of him.
"He saved others," they said, "but he cannot save himself! He is the king of Israel! Let him come down now from the cross, and then we will believe in him.
He trusts in God. Let God rescue him now if he wants him. After all, he said, 'I am the Son of God.'"
In the same way, the robbers who were on crosses next to him also insulted him.
From twelve o'clock until three o'clock in the afternoon, darkness covered the whole land.
At about three o'clock Jesus cried out in a loud voice, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?" This means, "My God, my God, why have you left me all alone?"
Some of the people standing there heard this. They said, "He is calling for Elijah."
Straight away one of them ran and got a sponge. He filled it with sour wine, put it on a stick and offered it to Jesus to drink.
The rest said, "Leave him alone. Let's see if Elijah comes to save him."
Jesus cried out again in a loud voice, and he gave up his spirit.
At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. The earth shook, and the rocks split.
Tombs broke open, and the bodies of many of God's people who had died were raised to life.
They came out of the tombs after Jesus rose from the dead. They went into the holy city and appeared to many people.
The Roman officer and the soldiers who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and everything that had happened. They were terrified and said, "He really was the Son of God!"
Many women were there, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee to take care of his needs.
Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's sons.
As evening came, a rich man from Arimathea arrived. His name was Joseph, and he had also become a follower of Jesus.
He went to Pilate and asked for Jesus' body, and Pilate ordered that it be given to him.
Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.
He placed it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out of the rock. He rolled a big stone in front of the entrance to the tomb and went away.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there across from the tomb.
The next day, the day after Preparation Day, the chief priests and the Pharisees went to Pilate.
"Sir," they said, "we remember that while that liar was still alive he said, 'After three days I will rise again.'

So give the order to make the tomb secure until the third day. If you do not, his followers may come and steal the body. Then they will tell the people that he has been raised from the dead. This last lie will be worse than the first."
"Take some guards," Pilate answered. "Go and make the tomb as secure as you know how."
So they went and made the tomb secure. They put a seal on the stone and placed guards there.
